name: gunicorn_h1c
baseline: httptools (MagicStack, llhttp-based) / CPython pure-Python HTTP parser
workload: Simple GET request parsing loop, requests/sec on Apple M4 Pro (single thread), comparing gunicorn_h1c (a picohttpparser wrapper with added SIMD) against httptools and a pure-Python parser
claimed_speedup: gunicorn_h1c (fast): ~2,500,000 req/s; gunicorn_h1c (H1CProtocol, reused): ~4,700,000 req/s; vs httptools: ~2,200,000 req/s; vs Pure Python: ~150,000 req/s
tradeoffs: Python C-extension wrapping picohttpparser with hand-added SIMD (SSE4.2/NEON); zero-copy with lazy Python object creation; only wraps request/response line + header parsing, not a full server; GitHub license detector shows NOASSERTION despite an included MIT LICENSE file
caveats: Numbers are a README table with no compiler flags and no benchmark script reproducing the httptools/Pure-Python rows (only an internal callback-vs-pull-API microbenchmark script is in the repo); httptools wraps llhttp so this is an indirect llhttp comparison, not a direct one; very low star count
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "url parser" simd (also found via "http/1.1 parser" simd)

name: milo
workload: autocannon HTTP load test against a Node.js native-addon HTTP server using milo vs the same server using llhttp for parsing ("preliminary" test, one run each)
claimed_speedup: milo avg 30,765.1 req/s (338k requests in 11.02s) vs llhttp avg 28,808 req/s (317k requests in 11.02s) -- about 1.07x faster; talk text summarizes: "Milo matches or outperforms llhttp in native mode"
tradeoffs: Rust state-machine parser generated via proc-macros, compiles to native or WASM; explicitly stricter than llhttp (rejects HTTP/0.9, HTTP/1.0, RTSP, obs-fold, bare LF/CR, bodies on GET/HEAD); author states it is slower than llhttp when compiled to WebAssembly; project goal is to replace llhttp as Node.js's HTTP parser
caveats: Numbers come from a conference-talk slide deck (autocannon output pasted as text), explicitly labelled "Performance in Node (native, preliminary)" -- no CPU model, no compiler/build flags, single run, not reproduced in the repo's own README or benchmark folder. This is the same milo the orchestrator flagged as having a harness but no published numbers; these numbers were found in the linked talk deck, not the repo itself.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "outperforms llhttp" -> ShogunPanda/talks src/talks/milo/slides.yml

name: liburlparser (abspath fast-path vs ada)
workload: Single-process, interleaved A/B/C micro-benchmark of abspath() ('.'/'..' path normalization) calls/sec, liburlparser (old unfixed, new fixed) vs unmodified ada::url_aggregator, 12 interleaved rounds
claimed_speedup: liburlparser NEW: ~7.4-7.8M ops/s vs ada: ~6.0-6.1M ops/s => ~1.24-1.29x faster than ada on this operation (liburlparser OLD was ~0.90-0.91x, i.e. slower, before the fix)
tradeoffs: Only the abspath()-only micro-benchmark beats ada; the project's own OPTIMIZATION_NOTES.md says overall parse_url is still ~17.9% behind ada after this and other fixes, so the library as a whole is currently slower than ada, not faster -- only this specific sub-operation wins. Adds Public Suffix List domain extraction that ada does not have.
caveats: No CPU model or compiler flags stated ("this machine", 3 runs); LICENSE file text is pybind11's BSD-3-Clause boilerplate with a mismatched copyright holder, and GitHub's license detector reports NOASSERTION/Other -- treat the OSI-approved classification as based on the license text itself, not the (possibly copy-pasted) attribution; the headline win is one micro-op, not the parser as a whole
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "vs ada-url" -> MohammadRaziei/liburlparser benchmarks/cpp/abspath_fix_verification

name: blazehttp
workload: Go micro-benchmark of HTTP/1.1 request header parsing at three sizes (1 header, 8 headers, 20 headers), ns/op and allocs/op, BlazeHTTP's zero-alloc parser vs fasthttp's request parser
claimed_speedup: Simple GET (1 header): 252ns/0 allocs vs fasthttp 1,336ns/1 alloc = 5.3x; Typical (8 headers): 2,377ns/0 allocs vs 6,198ns/1 alloc = 2.6x; Many headers (20): 4,776ns/0 allocs vs 10,077ns/1 alloc = 2.1x. (Whole-server wrk benchmarks in the same README also show BlazeHTTP +10.6% to +13.6% req/s over fasthttp on HTTP/1.1, and +56.9% to +133.9% over net/http on HTTP/2.)
tradeoffs: From-scratch Go HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2 implementation adding TLS/HTTP2 fingerprint evasion (JA3/JA4, browser emulation) that fasthttp does not attempt; fasthttp still lacks HTTP/2 entirely so the HTTP/2 numbers compare against net/http instead; only one external dependency (uTLS)
caveats: No CPU model, no compiler/Go-version flags, no raw benchmark source file linked (numbers are a README table only, tools named as wrk/h2load for the server-level tests but unstated for the ns/op header-parsing table); very low star count (2) and a single committer window in Feb 2026
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than net/http" parser -> justIliane/blazehttp
